big-o.blurb: What Big-O, Big-Ω and Big-Θ actually claim, how to compare growth rates, and the counting habits that make complexity analysis fast and right.

amortized.blurb: Why a dynamic array's append is O(1) even though some appends copy everything, and the three ways (aggregate, accounting, potential) to prove cheap-on-average costs.

recurrences.blurb: Turn recursive code into a recurrence, then solve it with the recursion tree or the Master theorem. The skill that lets you state divide-and-conquer complexity in seconds.

space-recursion.blurb: Memory is part of the answer: auxiliary space, the recursion stack, in-place tricks and the stack-overflow trap that bites recursive DFS on large inputs.

constraints-budget.blurb: Read the constraints first: n ≤ 20, 10³, 10⁵ or 10⁹ each point to a different family of algorithms. The fastest way to find the intended approach and to know when you are done.

dynamic-arrays.blurb: Contiguous memory, O(1) indexing, amortised O(1) append and O(n) middle inserts. Why arrays win on real hardware, and the operations that quietly cost linear time.

hash-tables.blurb: How a hash map really works: hash functions, buckets, chaining versus open addressing, load factor and resizing, and the worst cases interviewers like to probe.

counting-patterns.blurb: Frequency maps, "seen" sets, complement lookups and majority voting: the small toolkit behind most easy and medium array problems.

prefix-sums.blurb: Precompute cumulative sums once and answer any range sum in O(1). The 2D version, difference arrays for range updates, and prefix products.

prefix-hash.blurb: Count or find subarrays with a target sum (or remainder, or balance) in one pass by storing earlier prefix values in a hash map. Works with negatives, where sliding windows fail.

kadane.blurb: Maximum subarray in one pass: at each position, extend the best run ending here or start fresh. The smallest example of dynamic programming, with circular and product variants.

opposite-pointers.blurb: Two indices start at both ends of sorted data and move inward. Each step discards a whole row of candidate pairs, which is why O(n²) pair problems become O(n).

same-direction-pointers.blurb: A slow write pointer and a fast read pointer moving the same way: filter, compact, deduplicate and merge in place in one pass.

array-partition.blurb: Rearrange in place around a pivot or into colour classes: Lomuto and Hoare partitions and Dijkstra's three-way Dutch national flag.

merge-pointers.blurb: One pointer per sorted sequence, always advancing the smaller: merging, intersecting and comparing in linear time.

fixed-window.blurb: A window of exactly k elements slides one step at a time: add the new element, remove the old one, and keep the answer updated in O(1) per step.

variable-window.blurb: Grow the right edge, shrink the left edge while the window is invalid. Works whenever validity is monotone: if a window is valid, every smaller window inside it is too (or the reverse).

count-windows.blurb: Count subarrays instead of finding one: every valid window ending at r contributes r − l + 1, and "exactly k" is at-most(k) minus at-most(k − 1).

window-structures.blurb: When the window must answer max, min, median or "any value within t", pair the two pointers with a deque, two heaps or an ordered set.

stack-parsing.blurb: Last in, first out: matching brackets, evaluating expressions, decoding nested strings and simplifying paths. Whenever structure nests, a stack remembers where you came from.

monotonic-stack.blurb: Keep a stack whose values stay increasing (or decreasing). Each element is pushed and popped once, and every pop answers "what is the next greater (or smaller) element?" in O(n) total.

histogram.blurb: Largest rectangle under a histogram in O(n) with a monotonic stack, and the matrix version that runs it once per row.

stack-design.blurb: Augmented stacks and adapters: O(1) getMin, a max stack, queues from stacks and stacks from queues, and frequency stacks.

queues-deques.blurb: FIFO queues, double-ended queues and circular buffers: the structure behind BFS, schedulers and streams, and how each language implements them.

monotonic-deque.blurb: A deque whose values stay sorted, with expired indices dropped from the front: sliding-window maximum in O(n), and the shortest subarray with sum at least k even with negatives.

deque-dp.blurb: When a DP transition takes the best of the previous k states, a monotonic deque turns O(n·k) into O(n).

bs-boundaries.blurb: Binary search as "find the first index where a predicate turns true". One invariant-driven template that handles lower bound, upper bound, first/last occurrence and insert position without off-by-one bugs.

bs-rotated.blurb: Rotated sorted arrays, peaks and arrays of unknown size: binary search still works because one half is always sorted, or because the slope tells you which way is up.

bs-answer.blurb: When checking a candidate answer is easy but finding it directly is hard, binary search over the answer space: feasibility is monotone, so the smallest feasible value is a first-true search.

bs-2d-median.blurb: Binary search in matrices (flattened, or row and column sorted) and the hardest classic: the median of two sorted arrays in O(log min(m, n)) by binary searching a partition.

bs-real-ternary.blurb: Binary search on real numbers (bisection) and ternary search for the peak of a unimodal function, with the precision traps that come with floating point.

ll-basics.blurb: Nodes and pointers: traversal, insertion and deletion, the dummy head that removes edge cases, and why linked lists are rarer in practice than in interviews.

ll-reversal.blurb: Reverse a list in place with three pointers, then reuse the same move for sublists, k-groups, pairs and palindrome checks.

fast-slow.blurb: Two pointers moving at speeds 1 and 2: find the middle, detect a cycle and its entrance (Floyd), and solve "find the duplicate number" without modifying the array.

ll-merge-sort.blurb: Merging sorted lists, merging k of them, and sorting a linked list in O(n log n) with merge sort: the one sort that suits lists naturally.

ll-copy-design.blurb: Deep copies with random pointers, flattening multilevel lists, and the list-plus-map designs (LRU, browser history) that need O(1) moves.

tree-traversals.blurb: Pre-, in-, post- and level-order: recursive, iterative with an explicit stack, and Morris traversal in O(1) space. Choosing the order is choosing when you do the work.

tree-dfs-returns.blurb: The single most useful tree skill: define what a recursive call returns, compute it from the children, and update a global answer on the side. Height, diameter, balanced, max path sum and friends.

tree-bfs.blurb: Level-order traversal with a queue: per-level processing, right-side view, zigzag, widths, cousins and distance-K problems (with parent pointers).

tree-construct.blurb: Build trees from traversals, serialise and deserialise them, and build balanced trees from sorted input. Index maps and recursion ranges make these O(n).

lca.blurb: Lowest common ancestor by recursion, by parent pointers, in a BST, and with binary lifting for many queries. The building block for distances and path queries on trees.

bst-ops.blurb: Search, insert and delete in a binary search tree, including the three deletion cases and why an unbalanced BST degrades to a linked list.

bst-inorder.blurb: In-order traversal of a BST is sorted, and that single fact solves validation, k-th smallest, recovering swapped nodes, iterators and two-sum on a BST.

balanced-bst.blurb: How AVL and red-black trees keep height O(log n) with rotations, why B-trees rule databases, and how to use ordered maps (TreeMap, std::map) in interviews.

trie-basics.blurb: A tree keyed by characters: insert and lookup in O(length), prefix queries for free, and the memory trade-offs between arrays and hash maps per node.

trie-search.blurb: Tries as search engines: Word Search II on a board, streaming suffix matches, palindrome pairs and autocomplete with ranking.

bit-trie.blurb: Store numbers bit by bit from the most significant bit and answer "maximum XOR with x" greedily in O(bits). Offline queries with limits sort first.

heap-internals.blurb: A complete binary tree in an array: sift up, sift down, why building a heap is O(n) not O(n log n), heap sort, and the API differences across languages.

top-k.blurb: k largest, k smallest, k closest, k most frequent and merging k sorted streams: a size-k heap, quickselect, or bucket sort, each with its own trade-off.

two-heaps.blurb: A max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half: the running median in O(log n) per insert, sliding medians with lazy deletion, and IPO-style two-pool problems.

heap-scheduling.blurb: Simulate time with heaps: meeting rooms, task schedulers with cooldowns, CPU queues, servers and events processed in order of availability.

indexed-pq.blurb: When priorities change: lazy deletion with stale entries, indexed priority queues with decrease-key, and when an ordered set is the simpler tool.

subsets-combinations.blurb: Enumerate choices with a recursion tree: choose, explore, un-choose. Subsets, combinations and combination sums, with the duplicate-handling and pruning rules that keep them correct and fast.

permutations.blurb: Arrange all elements: used-flags or in-place swapping, duplicate handling with a sorted skip rule, and next_permutation for lexicographic order without recursion.

constraint-search.blurb: N-Queens, Sudoku and other constraint puzzles: place, check constraints in O(1) with bookkeeping, and prune early. The craft is in the bookkeeping and the order of choices.

grid-backtracking.blurb: DFS over a grid that marks cells on the path and unmarks them on return: word search, unique paths through obstacles, gold collection, with pruning that makes it pass.

partition-backtracking.blurb: Split a string or array into pieces that each satisfy a rule: palindrome partitioning, k equal-sum subsets and matchsticks, with memoisation and ordering tricks.

graph-representations.blurb: Adjacency lists, adjacency matrices and edge lists: what each costs, when to use which, and how to build graphs from the messy inputs interviews give you.

bfs.blurb: Breadth-first search explores in waves of increasing distance, so the first time it reaches a vertex is along a shortest path (in edges). The workhorse for unweighted shortest paths.

dfs.blurb: Depth-first search goes deep before wide. Discovery and finish times, the four edge types, connected components, and why DFS (not BFS) is the engine behind cycles, topological order, bridges and SCCs.

cycle-detection.blurb: Undirected: a visited neighbour that is not your parent, or a union-find merge that fails. Directed: a back edge to a grey vertex, or Kahn's algorithm leaving vertices behind.

grid-graphs.blurb: Grids are graphs with implicit edges: direction arrays, bounds checks, flood fill, multi-source BFS for nearest distances, and when to mark cells in place.

bipartite.blurb: Can vertices be split into two sides with every edge crossing? Two-colour with BFS or DFS; an odd cycle is the only obstacle. The gateway to matching.

state-space-bfs.blurb: When vertices are configurations (lock codes, board states, (cell, keys) pairs), BFS over the implicit graph finds the minimum number of moves. Design the state, then run plain BFS.

kahn.blurb: Repeatedly take a vertex with no remaining prerequisites. Kahn's algorithm orders a DAG in O(V + E), detects cycles for free, and adapts to "minimum semesters" and "lexicographically smallest order".

dfs-topo.blurb: Topological order as reversed DFS finish times: a vertex finishes only after everything it points to, so reversing finish order puts every edge left to right.

dag-dp.blurb: On a DAG, process vertices in topological order and every DP over paths becomes one linear pass: longest path, number of paths, critical path scheduling.

order-constraints.blurb: Infer a hidden order from evidence (sorted alien words, sequences, pairwise rules) by building a precedence graph and topologically sorting it, with the edge cases that make these problems hard.

dsu-core.blurb: Disjoint set union: find with path compression, union by rank or size, near-constant amortised time, and the inverse-Ackermann bound behind it.

dsu-applications.blurb: Union-find in the wild: merging accounts, equations, similar strings, stones and islands added over time. The trick is choosing what to union.

weighted-dsu.blurb: Union-find that also stores a relation to the parent (a ratio, an offset, a parity), so it can answer "what is a/b?" or "same or opposite team?" while merging.

offline-dsu.blurb: Sort queries and edges together, or run time backwards, so a structure that only supports merging can answer threshold and deletion problems.

dijkstra.blurb: Shortest paths from one source with non-negative weights: always settle the closest unsettled vertex. Heap implementation, correctness argument, and why negative edges break it.

zero-one-bfs.blurb: Edge weights only 0 or 1: a deque replaces Dijkstra's heap. Push 0-edges to the front and 1-edges to the back for O(V + E) shortest paths.

bellman-ford.blurb: Relax every edge V − 1 times: handles negative weights, detects negative cycles, and with a round limit solves "cheapest flight within K stops".

floyd-warshall.blurb: All-pairs shortest paths in three nested loops: allow intermediate vertices one at a time. O(V³), handles negative edges, and doubles as transitive closure.

state-dijkstra.blurb: Dijkstra where a vertex is a richer state (city + stops used, cell + coupons left) or the cost is not a plain sum (maximum edge, probability). The most common way shortest paths appear in Google interviews.

a-star.blurb: Dijkstra guided by a heuristic estimate of the remaining distance. Admissible and consistent heuristics keep it optimal; bidirectional search and contraction hierarchies are how real map routing scales.

dp-foundations.blurb: How to derive any DP instead of recalling it: brute-force recursion, find the changing parameters (the state), memoise, flip to a table, then compress space. Plus how to recognise DP and talk about it.

linear-dp.blurb: One index, a few look-backs: climbing stairs, house robber, decode ways, minimum cost tickets. The bread-and-butter DP family and its rolling-variable form.

state-machine-dp.blurb: Model each day as a transition between a few states (holding, not holding, cooling down, transactions left). The six stock problems become one template.

lis.blurb: Longest increasing subsequence in O(n²) DP and O(n log n) patience sorting, reconstruction, counting, and the disguises: Russian dolls, longest chain, minimum deletions.

partition-dp.blurb: Can the sequence be cut into valid pieces, and what is the best way to cut it? dp[i] over prefixes with a loop over the last piece: word break, palindrome cuts, splitting arrays.

grid-dp.blurb: dp[r][c] from the cell above and the cell to the left: unique paths, minimum path sum, maximal square, falling paths, and the two-walkers trick for cherry pickup.

two-sequence-dp.blurb: dp[i][j] over prefixes of two strings: longest common subsequence, edit distance, interleaving, wildcard and regex matching. One table shape, many problems.

palindrome-dp.blurb: Palindromic substrings and subsequences: expand around centres, the isPal table, longest palindromic subsequence as LCS with the reverse, and minimum insertions.

counting-dp.blurb: Count the ways rather than find the best: distinct subsequences, dice rolls, paths with constraints, and the mod-arithmetic and double-counting traps.

knapsack-01.blurb: Each item at most once, capacity W: dp over (items, capacity), the reverse loop that makes one array enough, and why the O(nW) algorithm is pseudo-polynomial.

knapsack-unbounded.blurb: Unlimited copies of each item: iterate capacity upwards. Coin change (minimum coins and number of ways), rod cutting and perfect squares.

subset-sum.blurb: Can a subset reach exactly a target? Boolean knapsack, bitset speed-ups, and the classic reductions: equal partition, target sum with signs, minimum subset difference.

knapsack-variants.blurb: Bounded counts, groups where you pick one per group, dependencies, and value-indexed DP when capacities are huge: the knapsack variants that appear as hard follow-ups.

interval-dp.blurb: dp[l][r] over every interval, with a loop over the split point: burst balloons, matrix chain multiplication, minimum cost to cut a stick, optimal BSTs. O(n³), filled by increasing length.

bitmask-dp.blurb: When n ≤ 20, a subset fits in an integer: dp over masks for travelling salesman, assignment, visiting all nodes and partitioning, in O(2ⁿ · n) or O(2ⁿ · n²).

tree-dp.blurb: DP where the state is a tree node: include/exclude a node (house robber III), subtree sizes and sums, rerooting to get every node's answer in O(n), and knapsack on trees.

game-dp.blurb: Two optimal players: minimax over states, score differences instead of two totals, win/lose positions, Nim and Sprague–Grundy numbers for sums of games.

digit-dp.blurb: Count numbers in [L, R] with a digit property by walking digits from the most significant with a "tight" flag. Turns 10¹⁸ ranges into a few thousand states.

dp-optimizations.blurb: When the transition is the bottleneck: monotone queues, convex hull trick, divide and conquer and Knuth optimisations, and matrix exponentiation for linear recurrences.

greedy-proofs.blurb: Make the locally best choice and never look back, but only after proving it safe. Exchange arguments, "greedy stays ahead", and the counterexamples that send you to DP.

greedy-reach.blurb: Track the farthest point you can reach (jump game), or the running surplus (gas station). One linear pass replaces a quadratic DP.

greedy-heap.blurb: Greedy choices that need the best remaining option at every step: Huffman coding, merging ropes or stones, reorganising strings, IPO and course scheduling.

greedy-sorting.blurb: Sort by the right key, then sweep: boats, assigning tasks to workers, maximum units on a truck, reducing arrays. The key is the whole insight.

merge-intervals.blurb: Sort by start, then merge whenever the next interval starts before the current one ends. Insert, merge, intersect and remove intervals with the boundary conventions stated.

sweep-line.blurb: Turn intervals into +1/−1 events at their endpoints and sweep in order: maximum overlap, meeting rooms, car pooling, and the tie-breaking rule that decides touching intervals.

interval-scheduling.blurb: Choose the most non-overlapping intervals (earliest end first), remove the fewest to make the rest disjoint, burst balloons with the fewest arrows, and weighted scheduling with DP.

skyline.blurb: The Skyline Problem and its relatives: a sweep over building edges with a multiset (or heap with lazy deletion) of active heights, emitting a key point whenever the maximum changes.

bit-basics.blurb: Bitwise operators, two's complement, shifts and the idioms (lowest set bit, clear lowest bit, test/set/toggle) that interviewers expect you to write without thinking.

xor-tricks.blurb: x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x: find the single number, the missing number, two unique numbers, and XOR over prefixes and ranges.

bitmask-enum.blurb: Represent subsets as integers: enumerate all subsets, iterate submasks, use masks as compact sets of letters or visited states.

bit-counting.blurb: Count set bits for a single number, for every number up to n with DP, and in Hamming-distance sums using per-bit contributions.

gcd-primes.blurb: Euclid's GCD and why it is fast, LCM without overflow, primality by trial division, the sieve of Eratosthenes, and prime factorisation for divisor problems.

modular.blurb: Arithmetic modulo 10⁹ + 7: safe addition and multiplication, fast exponentiation, modular inverses via Fermat, and why the modulus is prime.

combinatorics.blurb: Counting without enumerating: permutations, combinations, stars and bars, Catalan numbers, inclusion–exclusion and the pigeonhole principle.

geometry.blurb: Points, lines and polygons with integers only: cross products for orientation, segment intersection, polygon area (shoelace), convex hull, and Max Points on a Line.

randomized.blurb: Fisher–Yates shuffle, reservoir sampling for streams, weighted random picks with prefix sums, rejection sampling, and randomised algorithms like quickselect.

string-basics.blurb: Immutability and builders, character counts, anagram and palindrome checks, encoding and parsing: the everyday string skills and the hidden quadratic traps.

rolling-hash.blurb: Hash every substring in O(1) after O(n) preprocessing: Rabin–Karp search, repeated substrings with binary search, and the collision risks you must manage.

kmp.blurb: The prefix function (failure function) and the Knuth–Morris–Pratt matcher: linear-time search that never re-reads text, plus periods, borders and the shortest palindrome trick.

z-algorithm.blurb: Z[i] = length of the longest substring starting at i that matches a prefix. Linear time with a sliding [l, r) box; pattern search, periods and string compression follow.

manacher.blurb: All maximal palindromes in O(n): mirror palindrome radii inside the rightmost known palindrome. The linear answer to longest palindromic substring.

suffix-structures.blurb: Suffix arrays with LCP, suffix automata and Aho–Corasick: the heavy machinery for distinct substrings, longest repeats and multi-pattern matching, and how to talk about them in interviews.

sparse-table.blurb: Precompute minimums over power-of-two lengths and answer range-minimum queries in O(1) with two overlapping blocks. Static data only.

fenwick.blurb: A binary indexed tree: prefix sums with point updates in O(log n) using the lowest set bit, in about ten lines. Inversion counts, counting smaller elements and range-update variants.

segment-tree.blurb: A tree over array ranges supporting range queries and point updates in O(log n) for any associative operation, with the recursive and iterative implementations and how to design node merges.

lazy-propagation.blurb: Range updates in O(log n): store pending updates on nodes and push them to children only when needed. Range add, range assign, and composing tags correctly.

sqrt-mo.blurb: Split the array into √n blocks for O(√n) updates and queries, and Mo's algorithm for offline range queries by sorting them cleverly.

lru-lfu.blurb: LRU: hash map + doubly linked list for O(1) get and put. LFU: frequency buckets with a minimum-frequency pointer. The most asked design-a-data-structure questions.

iterators.blurb: Lazy iteration with hasNext/next: flatten nested lists, peeking iterators, zigzag over several sources, and iterators over trees, all with O(1) amortised steps and small memory.

time-versioned.blurb: Key-value stores with timestamps and snapshots: binary search over per-key histories, snapshot arrays that store only changes, and stock-price style correction streams.

randomized-set.blurb: Insert, delete and getRandom in O(1): an array for uniform sampling plus a hash map from value to index, deleting by swapping with the last element.

stream-counters.blurb: Designs over event streams: hit counters, loggers, moving averages, rate limiters and medians, with queues, circular buckets and the trade-offs systems interviews probe next.

skiplist.blurb: A probabilistic alternative to balanced trees: layered linked lists with expected O(log n) search, insert and delete. How Redis sorted sets and LevelDB memtables work.

matrix-traversal.blurb: Spiral, diagonal and layer-by-layer traversals, in-place rotation by transpose-and-reverse, and boundary bookkeeping that avoids off-by-one errors.

matrix-in-place.blurb: Mark changes without extra memory: reuse the first row and column as flags (Set Matrix Zeroes), encode old and new states in one cell (Game of Life), and simulate on the grid itself.

matrix-search.blurb: Searching sorted matrices: flatten for fully sorted, staircase from a corner for row-and-column sorted, and value binary search with counting for k-th smallest.

comparison-sorts.blurb: Merge sort, quicksort and heapsort: how they work, their worst cases, stability and memory, and what real libraries (Timsort, introsort, pdqsort) actually do.

linear-sorts.blurb: Beat n log n by not comparing: counting sort for small key ranges, radix sort digit by digit, bucket sort for uniform data, and pigeonhole tricks like Maximum Gap.

quickselect.blurb: Find the k-th smallest in expected O(n) by partitioning and recursing on one side only. Median-of-medians guarantees O(n) worst case; introselect combines both.

custom-sort.blurb: Comparators that encode the problem (largest number, custom orders), stability for multi-key sorts, and counting inversions during merge sort.

meet-in-middle.blurb: Split n ≤ 40 items into two halves, enumerate 2^(n/2) subsets of each, and combine with sorting, hashing or two pointers: 2⁴⁰ becomes about 2·10⁶.

heavy-light.blurb: Decompose a tree into heavy paths so any root-to-node path crosses O(log n) of them; combine with a segment tree for path queries and updates. Centroid decomposition for distance queries.

persistent.blurb: Keep every version of a structure by copying only the changed path: persistent arrays, stacks and segment trees, and the k-th smallest in a range trick.

randomized-structures.blurb: Treaps (BST by key, heap by random priority) with split and merge, and splay trees: balanced in expectation or amortised, with simple code for ordered sets with extra operations.

mst.blurb: Connect every vertex at the least total cost. Two greedy algorithms, one theorem (the cut property) that makes both correct, and a family of disguises from clustering to bottleneck paths.

bridges-ap.blurb: Which single link, or single machine, takes the network down? One DFS with two timestamps per vertex answers both, and the same idea underpins biconnected components.

scc.blurb: In a directed graph, which vertices can all reach each other? Two linear-time algorithms find these components, and contracting them turns any directed graph into a DAG you can sort and run DP on.

euler.blurb: Walk every edge exactly once. The existence test is pure degree counting, and Hierholzer's algorithm builds the walk in linear time by appending vertices on the way back.

network-flow.blurb: How much can you push from a source to a sink through capacity-limited pipes? Max-flow equals min-cut, augmenting paths compute it, and bipartite matching, disjoint paths and assignment all reduce to it.

sd-round.blurb: What actually happens in a system design interview at Google, minute by minute, and what separates an L4 answer from an L5 and an L6 one.

sd-requirements.blurb: Turning "design X" into a precise problem: the few features that matter, what is deliberately left out, and the targets for scale, speed, availability and correctness that every later decision depends on.

sd-api-data.blurb: Before drawing servers, pin down the operations the system offers and the records it stores, because how data is looked up decides the database, the keys and the partitioning.

sd-deep-dives.blurb: The part of the interview that decides your level: finding the genuinely hard parts yourself, going two levels down, and explaining how the system behaves at peak load and when each piece fails.

latency-numbers.blurb: The handful of speed and size numbers that let you judge a design in your head: how long memory, disks and networks take, how much a machine can do, and how the times feel when scaled to human life.

capacity-math.blurb: Back-of-the-envelope estimation done properly: from users to requests per second, storage per year and bandwidth, with round numbers, stated assumptions, and only the figures that change a design decision.

capacity-planning.blurb: From estimates to hardware: how many servers, shards, cache nodes and connections a design needs, with headroom for peaks and failures, and how to tell which resource runs out first.

queueing.blurb: Why systems get slow long before they are "full": Little's law, how waiting time explodes as utilisation nears 100%, why tail latency dominates at scale, and the tricks (hedging, timeouts, shedding) that keep the tail short.

tcp-udp.blurb: How data actually crosses the internet: packets, the reliable ordered stream TCP builds on top of them, the bare-bones UDP, and QUIC, the modern transport that powers HTTP/3. What each costs in round trips, and when to use which.

http-tls.blurb: The language of the web and how it got faster: HTTP requests and responses, what TLS does to keep them private and authentic, and how HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 differ in connections, multiplexing and head-of-line blocking.

dns.blurb: How a name like maps.google.com becomes an IP address: the chain of resolvers and servers involved, caching and TTLs, the record types that matter, and how DNS is used (and limited) for routing users to the nearest data centre and for failover.

api-styles.blurb: REST, gRPC and GraphQL compared the way an interviewer expects: what each one is, how a request looks, where each shines and hurts, and which to choose for public APIs, internal services, mobile apps and streaming.

api-design.blurb: The details that separate a toy API from a production one: resource naming, cursor pagination, idempotency keys for safe retries, versioning, consistent errors, rate-limit signals and long-running operations.

realtime-push.blurb: How a server tells clients about new events: short polling, long polling, server-sent events and WebSockets compared on delay, cost and complexity, and how to run millions of persistent connections (routing, presence, heartbeats, reconnect storms).

l4-l7.blurb: What a load balancer is, why every scalable system has one, and the big fork in the road: balancing at layer 4 (connections, by address and port) or at layer 7 (requests, reading the HTTP inside), with what each can see, do and cost.

lb-algorithms.blurb: How a load balancer picks a server: round robin, weighted, random, least connections, least response time and the power of two choices, with a live race showing why load-blind strategies wreck tail latency and why "pick the least loaded" can stampede.

lb-health.blurb: How load balancers notice broken servers and stop sending them traffic: active and passive health checks, how long detection takes and what users suffer meanwhile, liveness vs readiness, connection draining for safe deploys, and the trap of health checks that take the whole fleet down.

api-gateway.blurb: The front door for many services: what an API gateway does on every request (authentication, rate limiting, routing, transformation, observability), how it differs from a load balancer and a service mesh, and how to keep it from becoming a slow single point of failure.

global-lb.blurb: Getting users worldwide to a nearby, healthy region: GeoDNS and anycast compared, terminating connections at the edge and riding a private backbone, and what happens to traffic and data when a whole region fails.

cache-patterns.blurb: The four ways an application and a cache can share the work of reading and writing (cache-aside, read-through, write-through and write-back), what each guarantees, what each loses when something crashes, and which to pick.

cache-eviction.blurb: When the cache is full, something must go: LRU, LFU, FIFO, random and modern admission policies like TinyLFU, raced on real access patterns, plus how to size a cache from the working set and the hit-rate curve.

cache-invalidation.blurb: "There are only two hard things in computer science": why keeping a cache in step with the database is genuinely hard, the race conditions that leave stale data forever, and the fixes used at scale (TTLs, delete-on-write, leases, versioning, change-data-capture invalidation).

cache-failures.blurb: How caches fail under load: stampedes when a hot key expires, penetration by requests for keys that do not exist, avalanches when many keys expire together or a cache node dies, and hot keys too popular for one server, each with the standard defences.

redis-memcached.blurb: Inside the two workhorse caches: Memcached's simple multithreaded slab-allocated key-value store, Redis's single-threaded data-structure server with persistence and replication, how each is scaled across many machines, and when to choose which.

cdn.blurb: Content delivery networks in depth: why serving from the edge matters, how CDN caching is controlled (cache keys, Cache-Control, purges, versioned URLs), origin shields, protecting private content with signed URLs, and what CDNs do for dynamic traffic.

sql-nosql.blurb: Choosing a database the way senior engineers do: from the access patterns, consistency needs and scale of each kind of data, not from "SQL vs NoSQL" slogans, with the trade-offs of relational, key-value, document, wide-column, graph, search and time-series stores.

data-modeling.blurb: Designing tables and keys for real access patterns: normalisation and when to break it, one-to-many and many-to-many relationships, choosing primary keys, modelling for key-value and wide-column stores, and handling counters, history and soft deletes.

db-indexes.blurb: How a database finds rows without reading the whole table: B-tree indexes, why the order of columns in a composite index matters, covering indexes, what each index costs on writes, and how to reason about a slow query.

btree-lsm.blurb: The two designs at the heart of almost every database's storage engine: B-trees that update pages in place, and log-structured merge trees that only append and merge in the background, with their read, write and space amplification and which workloads favour each.

olap-columnar.blurb: Why analytics needs different storage from the transactional app: OLTP vs OLAP, column-oriented storage and compression, data warehouses and lakes, and how data flows from production databases to analytics without hurting users.

nosql-families.blurb: A closer look at how the main non-relational stores work inside and how you design for them: key-value stores like DynamoDB, document stores like MongoDB and Firestore, wide-column stores like Bigtable and Cassandra, and graph databases, with their partitioning, consistency options and design rules.

leader-replication.blurb: Keeping copies of a database on several machines with one leader: how changes flow to followers, synchronous vs asynchronous replication, replication lag, and what really happens during failover, including lost writes and split brain.

multi-leader-leaderless.blurb: Letting more than one replica accept writes: multi-leader replication across data centres and offline devices, leaderless (Dynamo-style) replication where clients write to several replicas, the conflicts both create, and how they are resolved.

quorums.blurb: The arithmetic behind replicated reads and writes: N, W and R, why R + W > N gives overlap, what it does not guarantee, sloppy quorums and hinted handoff during failures, and how to choose the numbers for speed, availability and freshness.

consistency-models.blurb: What "consistent" can mean for replicated data, from strongest to weakest: linearisability, sequential, causal and eventual consistency, explained with concrete histories, and what each costs in latency and availability.

session-guarantees.blurb: Making eventually consistent systems feel right to each user: read-your-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes and consistent prefix reads, the anomalies each prevents, and the routing and versioning tricks that implement them.

cap-pacelc.blurb: What the CAP theorem actually says (and the many things it doesn't), why the real choice is what to do during a network partition, PACELC's addition of the latency-versus-consistency trade-off in normal operation, and how to talk about CP and AP systems precisely.

partition-schemes.blurb: Splitting data across machines when it no longer fits or no longer keeps up on one: range partitioning, hash partitioning and directory-based placement, what each makes cheap and expensive, and how to pick a partition key.

consistent-hashing.blurb: How to assign keys to servers so that adding or removing a server moves only a small share of keys: the hash ring, virtual nodes for balance, rendezvous (highest-random-weight) hashing, Google's jump and Maglev hashing, and bounded loads.

hot-keys.blurb: When one key, one partition or one user gets a huge share of traffic: detecting skew, the celebrity problem in feeds and counters, and the toolbox of salting, splitting, local caching, write batching and special-casing big accounts.

partitioned-indexes.blurb: Querying partitioned data by something other than its key: local (document-partitioned) indexes that need scatter-gather reads, global (term-partitioned) indexes that need cross-partition writes, and how real systems keep them in sync.

rebalancing.blurb: Moving data when machines are added, removed or overloaded, without downtime: fixed numbers of partitions, dynamic splitting and merging, how a partition is moved safely while it keeps serving, and who decides (automatic vs operator-driven).

unique-ids.blurb: Generating unique identifiers across many machines without a central bottleneck: auto-increment and its limits, UUIDs (v4 and time-ordered v7), Twitter's Snowflake layout, ticket servers and ID ranges, and choosing by ordering, size and guessability.

acid-wal.blurb: What a database transaction promises (atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability), what each letter really means, and how the write-ahead log makes "all or nothing" and "never lost" true even when the power goes out mid-write.

isolation-anomalies.blurb: What goes wrong when transactions run at the same time: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, lost updates, write skew and phantoms, which isolation level prevents which, and the practical fixes (row locks, atomic updates, conditional writes, serialisable transactions).

mvcc-2pl.blurb: How databases actually implement isolation: two-phase locking (and deadlocks), multi-version concurrency control (readers never block writers), and serialisable snapshot isolation, with their costs in contention, aborts and garbage.

two-phase-commit.blurb: Committing one transaction across several databases or partitions: the two-phase commit protocol step by step, why it blocks when the coordinator fails, how real systems (Spanner) make it safe with consensus, and when to avoid it altogether.

sagas-outbox.blurb: Keeping data correct across services without distributed transactions: sagas (a chain of local transactions with compensations), orchestration vs choreography, the transactional outbox for reliably publishing events, and idempotent consumers.

consensus-raft.blurb: How a group of machines agrees on one ordered log despite crashes and network failures: the consensus problem, Raft's leader election, log replication and safety rules, how Paxos relates, and where consensus is used (etcd, ZooKeeper, Spanner, Chubby).

clocks-ordering.blurb: Why "what happened first?" is hard in distributed systems: physical clock skew, Lamport clocks, vector clocks, hybrid logical clocks, and Google's TrueTime with commit wait, and which ordering each one can and cannot give you.

distributed-locks.blurb: Making sure only one worker does something at a time across machines: leases instead of plain locks, why a paused process can still act after losing its lock, fencing tokens that make storage reject stale holders, and which lock services are safe for correctness.

queue-vs-log.blurb: Two kinds of asynchronous messaging that look alike and behave very differently: message queues (a job is handed to one worker and then gone) and logs (an ordered, durable record many consumers read at their own pace), and when to use each.

kafka-internals.blurb: How Kafka actually works: topics, partitions and keys, the append-only segment files that make it fast, leaders, in-sync replicas and acks, consumer groups and rebalancing, retention and compaction, and the numbers to size it.

delivery-semantics.blurb: At-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once delivery: where each comes from (when you commit your position relative to doing the work), why exactly-once is really "effectively once" built from at-least-once plus idempotence or transactions, and how to design consumers accordingly.

event-patterns.blurb: Designing with events: publish/subscribe fan-out, event notification vs event-carried state, event sourcing (store every change, derive state by replay), and CQRS (separate write and read models), with when each is worth its complexity.

retries-dlq.blurb: Keeping message processing healthy when things fail: per-key ordering vs parallelism, retries with backoff, poison messages and dead-letter queues, backpressure when consumers can't keep up, and handling duplicates and out-of-order delivery.

batch-processing.blurb: Processing huge, finished datasets: the MapReduce model (map, shuffle, reduce) that Google introduced, why it scales and tolerates failures, its successor Spark, and how to reason about the shuffle, skew and data locality.

stream-windows.blurb: Processing data that never ends: event time vs processing time, tumbling, sliding and session windows, why events arrive late and out of order, and how watermarks, triggers and allowed lateness decide when a window's answer is ready.

stateful-streams.blurb: Streams that remember: keyed state for counts, joins and deduplication, how processors checkpoint that state consistently (Chandy–Lamport-style barriers in Flink, Dataflow's exactly-once), and recovering without losing or double-counting events.

lambda-kappa.blurb: Two architectures for combining fresh and complete results: Lambda (a batch layer for correctness plus a speed layer for freshness) and Kappa (one streaming pipeline, reprocessing by replaying the log), with why the industry moved toward unified streaming.

cdc.blurb: Change data capture: turning a database's own commit log into a stream of row changes so search indexes, caches, warehouses and other services stay in sync without dual writes, with snapshotting, ordering, schema changes and the outbox variant.

rl-algorithms.blurb: The five classic rate-limiting algorithms (fixed window, sliding log, sliding window counter, token bucket, leaky bucket), raced on the same bursty traffic so you can see who lets a boundary burst through, who smooths, and what each costs in memory.

rl-distributed.blurb: Rate limiting when requests for the same client hit many servers: a central store with atomic operations, local counters synchronised periodically, sticky routing, and the accuracy-versus-latency trade-off, plus multi-region limits.

load-shedding.blurb: What to do when demand exceeds capacity: why overloaded systems collapse rather than slow down, retry storms and how retry budgets prevent them, load shedding and prioritisation, admission control, backpressure, and graceful degradation.

object-storage.blurb: Storing billions of files and petabytes of data cheaply and durably: how object stores like Google Cloud Storage work (flat keys, immutable objects, metadata vs data), replication vs erasure coding, eleven nines of durability, storage classes and direct uploads with signed URLs.

media-delivery.blurb: How video platforms turn an upload into smooth playback anywhere: chunked uploads, transcoding into a ladder of resolutions and bitrates, packaging into short segments (HLS/DASH), adaptive bitrate players, CDN delivery, and the costs that dominate.

inverted-index.blurb: How search engines find documents in milliseconds: tokenising text, building posting lists, intersecting them for queries, ranking with TF-IDF/BM25, and sharding an index across machines (by document vs by term), with how updates reach the index.

geo-indexes.blurb: Answering "what's near me?" fast: why a normal index can't, geohashes that turn 2D locations into sortable strings, quadtrees that adapt to density, Google's S2 cells, and how ride-hailing and maps systems use them, including the edge cases.

sketches.blurb: Answering "is it in the set?", "how many distinct?" and "how often?" over huge streams with tiny memory and small, known errors: Bloom filters, HyperLogLog and Count-Min sketches, how each works and where large systems use them.

time-series.blurb: Storing metrics and other time-stamped data efficiently: the shape of time-series workloads, compression (delta-of-delta, XOR), downsampling and retention, the cardinality problem, and how systems like Prometheus and Google's Monarch are built.

slos.blurb: Defining "reliable enough" with numbers, the way Google's SRE practice does: service level indicators, objectives and agreements, error budgets that turn reliability into a resource you spend, and burn-rate alerts that page only when it matters.

resilience-patterns.blurb: The patterns that keep one failing component from taking down everything: timeouts and deadlines, retries done safely, circuit breakers, bulkheads, fallbacks and graceful degradation, and how they combine on a real request path.

observability.blurb: Understanding a running system from the outside: metrics for trends and alerts, logs for events and details, distributed traces for following one request across services, and how to instrument a design so incidents can be debugged quickly.

safe-deploys.blurb: Changing a running system without breaking it: rolling, blue-green and canary deployments, feature flags that separate deploy from release, backward-compatible schema changes, automated rollback, and why most outages start with a change.

failure-detection.blurb: Deciding that a machine is dead when you can't tell dead from slow: heartbeats and timeouts, the impossibility behind it, phi-accrual detectors, gossip-based membership (SWIM), and how detection speed trades against false alarms.

authn.blurb: Proving who a user or service is: sessions vs tokens, what a JWT is and what it isn't, OAuth 2.0 authorisation code flow with PKCE, OpenID Connect for login, refresh tokens and revocation, and service-to-service identity with mTLS.

authz.blurb: Deciding what an authenticated user may do: role-based (RBAC), attribute-based (ABAC) and relationship-based access control, Google's Zanzibar model of relation tuples behind Drive and YouTube sharing, and where authorisation checks belong in a design.

encryption.blurb: Protecting data in transit and at rest: TLS everywhere, encryption at rest with envelope encryption and a key management service, key rotation, end-to-end encryption, and hashing vs encryption vs signing, explained without cryptography maths.

multi-tenancy.blurb: Serving many customers from shared infrastructure safely: isolation models from shared tables to dedicated stacks, tenant IDs and data isolation, the noisy-neighbour problem with quotas and fair scheduling, tenant-aware sharding, and per-tenant keys and residency.

abuse-ddos.blurb: Keeping a public service up and fair under attack and abuse: volumetric and application-layer DDoS, anycast and edge absorption, WAFs, bot detection and proof-of-work-style challenges, account-level abuse (credential stuffing, spam) and layered defences.

region-topologies.blurb: Running one service from several regions of the world: why you'd do it (surviving a region failure, being close to users, keeping data in a country), the main shapes (active-passive and active-active, with read-local or write-local data), what each costs in latency, consistency and money, and how traffic moves when a region dies.

conflict-resolution.blurb: What to do when two places change the same data at the same time without talking to each other: last-writer-wins and what it silently throws away, version vectors that detect true concurrency, application merges, and CRDTs (counters, sets, registers and text) that merge automatically and always agree in the end.

disaster-recovery.blurb: Planning for the day something destroys data or a whole site: RPO and RTO as the two numbers that drive everything, backups versus replicas (replicas copy mistakes too), point-in-time recovery, the 3-2-1 rule, immutable backups against ransomware, and why an untested restore is not a backup.

data-residency.blurb: Keeping certain data inside a country or region because a law or a customer contract says so: what residency and sovereignty mean, how geo-partitioning gives each user or tenant a home region, what can and can't leave (backups, logs, caches, support access, ML training), and how global features still work.

gfs-colossus.blurb: The Google File System (2003), which stored the web on thousands of cheap, failing disks with one master and 64 MB chunks, and Colossus, its successor: what each design choice bought, where the single master broke down, and which ideas (separating metadata from data, leases, pipelined writes, erasure coding) show up in every storage design since.

bigtable.blurb: Bigtable (2006), the sorted, sparse, multi-dimensional map behind Search, Maps, Gmail and Cloud Bigtable: rows, column families and timestamps, tablets that split as they grow, the log-structured write path on GFS, the three-level location lookup through Chubby, and how row-key design decides whether a table scales or melts one server.

spanner.blurb: Spanner (2012), Google's globally distributed SQL database: data split into Paxos-replicated groups, two-phase commit across groups, and TrueTime, a clock API with explicit uncertainty that lets Spanner give every transaction a timestamp consistent with real time by waiting out the uncertainty (commit wait). What external consistency means, why lock-free snapshot reads fall out of it, and what it costs.

chubby-zookeeper.blurb: Coordination services: Google's Chubby (2006) lock service and its open-source counterpart ZooKeeper (2010), which store tiny amounts of critical data with strong consistency so the rest of a system can elect leaders, hold locks, find each other and share configuration. Sessions, leases, ephemeral nodes, watches, sequencers, and the herd effect.

dynamo.blurb: Amazon's Dynamo (2007), the always-writable key-value store behind the shopping cart: consistent hashing with virtual nodes, a preference list of N replicas, sloppy quorums with hinted handoff, vector clocks with application merges, Merkle-tree anti-entropy and gossip membership. Why it chose availability over consistency, what Cassandra and Riak took from it, and why DynamoDB later moved away from it.

borg-kubernetes.blurb: Borg (2015), the cluster manager that runs nearly everything at Google, and Kubernetes, its open-source descendant: jobs and tasks, priorities and preemption, quotas, how the scheduler packs tasks onto machines, why sharing machines between serving and batch work saves so much, and the ideas Kubernetes kept (pods, labels, declarative desired state with reconcilers) and changed.

ood-at-google.blurb: What an object-oriented design question is, the three shapes it takes in real interviews (a "design a class" coding question, a dedicated design round, a longer machine-coding round), and what separates an L4, L5 and L6 answer.

ood-requirements.blurb: How to turn "design a library system" into a short list of actors and use cases, then into candidate classes (from nouns), methods (from verbs) and responsibilities, and finally into a small public API, before drawing anything.

class-diagrams.blurb: How to draw classes and the six relationships between them (association, aggregation, composition, dependency, inheritance, interface realisation) with multiplicities, what each one means in running code, and a light notation fast enough for a whiteboard.

behaviour-diagrams.blurb: The two diagrams that show behaviour rather than structure: sequence diagrams (who calls whom, in what order, for one flow) and state diagrams (the states an object can be in and the events that move it between them), with how each turns into code.

ood-core-code.blurb: What to code in the 15–20 minutes that matter: the entities that guard invariants, the interfaces where behaviour varies, the one or two key flows, named errors, and the tests you describe aloud, plus what the longer machine-coding format adds.

encapsulation.blurb: What a class really is (data plus the only operations allowed on it), why fields are private, and how encapsulation keeps a rule like "a balance never goes negative" true by checking it in exactly one place.

inheritance-composition.blurb: What inheritance really ties together, why "composition over inheritance" is the default advice, the combinatorial explosion that inheritance causes when behaviours combine, and the narrow cases where inheritance is the right tool.

polymorphism.blurb: What polymorphism is (one call, many behaviours), how dynamic dispatch picks the method at run time, interfaces versus abstract classes, overloading versus overriding, and generics for code that works over many types safely.

srp-ocp.blurb: The first two SOLID principles in practice: single responsibility (a class should have one reason to change, i.e. answer to one group of people) and open/closed (add behaviour by adding code, not by editing working code), with how to spot violations and fix them.

lsp-isp.blurb: Liskov substitution (a subtype must keep every promise its parent makes, or code using the parent breaks) with the rectangle/square and read-only-list traps, and interface segregation (small, role-shaped interfaces so no class implements methods it cannot support).

dip-di.blurb: Dependency inversion (business logic depends on interfaces it owns, and the database, clock and network adapters depend on those interfaces, not the other way round) and dependency injection (handing a class its collaborators instead of letting it create them), with constructor injection, composition roots, and why it makes code testable.

design-heuristics.blurb: The rules of thumb that sit beside SOLID: DRY (one source of truth for knowledge, not for look-alike code), KISS, YAGNI, the Law of Demeter, composition of small pure functions, and fail-fast, with how to use them without turning them into dogma.

factory-patterns.blurb: Why object creation deserves its own home, and the three factory shapes: a simple factory (one method that picks a class), the factory method (a subclass or strategy decides what to create), and the abstract factory (a family of objects that must match), with when each earns its place.

builder-prototype.blurb: The builder (assemble an object with many optional parts step by step, validate once, end up immutable) versus telescoping constructors and setter soup, and the prototype (create new objects by copying a configured one), with the shallow-versus-deep copy trap.

singleton-pool.blurb: The singleton (exactly one instance, globally reachable): how to write it safely in Java (holder idiom, enum, the double-checked-locking trap), why it is usually a disguised global variable that hurts testing, what to do instead, and object pools for expensive, reusable resources.

adapter-facade.blurb: Two wrappers with different purposes: the adapter (make an existing class fit the interface your code expects, typically around third-party libraries) and the facade (one simple entry point in front of a complicated subsystem), plus the anti-corruption layer idea that keeps outside models out of your domain.

decorator-proxy.blurb: Two same-interface wrappers: the decorator (stack extra behaviour such as logging, caching, retries or compression around an object, in any combination) and the proxy (stand in for an object to control access: lazy loading, remote calls, caching, permission checks), with how Java's I/O streams and dynamic proxies use them.

composite-bridge-flyweight.blurb: Three structural patterns for specific shapes of problem: composite (treat a tree of parts and wholes uniformly: files and folders, UI widgets, org charts), bridge (split two independent dimensions of variation so they combine instead of multiplying), and flyweight (share the heavy, unchanging part of many small objects to save memory).

strategy-template.blurb: Strategy (put an interchangeable algorithm behind an interface and inject it: pricing, routing, eviction, ranking) and template method (fix the steps of an algorithm in a base class and let subclasses fill in some of them), when to choose which, and how lambdas made strategies one line.

observer-pattern.blurb: Observer (a subject keeps a list of listeners and notifies them when something changes) for display boards, alerts and UI updates; push versus pull, synchronous versus asynchronous delivery, the memory-leak and slow-listener traps, and how it grows into an in-process event bus and publish/subscribe.

state-pattern.blurb: The state pattern (each state of an object is its own class that handles every event its own way, and decides the next state) for vending machines, elevators, orders and game turns; when it beats an enum with checks, how transitions are made thread-safe, and how a transition table helps when states are data.

command-memento.blurb: Command (turn a request into an object that can be queued, logged, undone or retried) and memento (capture an object's state as a snapshot without exposing its insides), and how they combine into undo/redo stacks for editors, drawing apps and transactions.

chain-of-responsibility.blurb: Chain of responsibility (pass a request along a line of handlers, each of which may handle it, change it, or stop it): middleware pipelines, logging levels, approval chains and request validation, with ordering, short-circuiting and how servlet filters and interceptors implement it.

iterator-visitor.blurb: Iterator (walk through a collection without knowing how it is stored: lazily, one element at a time, with hasNext/next) including fail-fast behaviour, and visitor (add new operations over a fixed set of node types without editing them, via double dispatch), with modern alternatives (generators, streams, sealed types with pattern matching).

mediator-null-object.blurb: Three smaller patterns that come up in LLD rounds: mediator (objects talk through one coordinator instead of to each other: chat rooms, auctions, air-traffic control, UI forms), null object (a do-nothing implementation instead of null checks), and interpreter (a tiny language as a tree of expression objects: rules, filters, formulas).

library-api.blurb: Designing the public API of a class or library that other engineers will call: naming, small surfaces, contracts (inputs, outputs, errors, thread safety, complexity), exceptions versus result types, nullability, immutability of inputs and outputs, and how to evolve an API without breaking callers.

modelling-data.blurb: How to model the data of a domain in code: entities (identity that lasts) versus value objects (defined by their values, immutable), enums for closed sets, IDs as types, money and time done right, and "make illegal states unrepresentable" with types instead of flags.

testability.blurb: Designing code that is easy to test: seams where dependencies can be swapped, the kinds of test doubles (dummy, stub, fake, spy, mock) and when to use each, why Google prefers fakes and real objects over heavy mocking, testing time and concurrency, and what to say when asked "how would you test this?".

smells-refactoring.blurb: The code smells interviewers and reviewers notice (long methods, god classes, feature envy, primitive obsession, switch statements, shotgun surgery, data clumps, comments explaining bad code) and the refactoring moves that fix each one safely, in small steps under tests.

code-layers.blurb: How code inside one service is organised into layers: presentation (controllers), application services (use cases), domain (entities and rules) and infrastructure (repositories, clients), the MVC pattern, the repository pattern, and hexagonal (ports and adapters) architecture, with the dependency rule that keeps business logic independent.

threads-basics.blurb: What processes and threads are, what they share, concurrency versus parallelism, how many threads actually run at once, the thread lifecycle and cost, and why I/O-bound and CPU-bound work need different numbers of threads.

race-conditions.blurb: What a race condition is, the two shapes it almost always takes (read-modify-write and check-then-act), why count++ loses updates, what a critical section and atomicity mean, and the four ways to fix a race.

memory-visibility.blurb: Why one thread's write may never be seen by another (CPU caches, store buffers, compiler and CPU reordering), the Java memory model's happens-before rule, what volatile, synchronized, final and thread start/join guarantee, and safe publication of objects.

locks.blurb: The lock toolbox: intrinsic locks (synchronized), ReentrantLock with tryLock, timeouts and fairness, read-write locks for read-heavy data, StampedLock's optimistic reads, lock granularity (one big lock versus fine-grained and striped locks), and the rules for holding locks safely.

condition-variables.blurb: How a thread waits efficiently for a condition to become true (an item in the queue, a free slot, a turn) instead of spinning: wait/notify, Condition objects, the "always wait in a while loop" rule, spurious and lost wake-ups, notify versus notifyAll, and building a bounded buffer.

deadlock.blurb: Deadlock (threads each holding what another needs, waiting forever), the four Coffman conditions and how breaking any one prevents it (lock ordering, tryLock with timeout, acquiring all at once), plus livelock and starvation, and how to find deadlocks with thread dumps.

atomics-cas.blurb: Lock-free building blocks: atomic variables and compare-and-set (CAS), the CAS retry loop, LongAdder for hot counters, AtomicReference for swapping immutable state, the ABA problem and how version stamps fix it, and when lock-free is (and isn't) worth it.

producer-consumer.blurb: The producer–consumer pattern: decoupling threads that make work from threads that do it with a bounded blocking queue, the BlockingQueue API (put/take/offer/poll), backpressure when consumers fall behind, poison pills and graceful shutdown, and the single most-asked concurrency coding question: implement a bounded blocking queue.

sync-primitives.blurb: The coordination tools beyond locks: semaphores (N permits: limit concurrency, build pools and bounded resources), countdown latches (wait until N things have happened), cyclic barriers and phasers (threads meet at a point before continuing), and exchangers, with what each is for.

thread-pools.blurb: Why programs use thread pools instead of creating threads, how Java's ThreadPoolExecutor works (core and maximum threads, the work queue, rejection policies), sizing pools, futures for results, shutdown, and the traps: unbounded queues, thread-starvation deadlock and lost exceptions.

concurrent-collections.blurb: The thread-safe collections you build components from: ConcurrentHashMap and its atomic compound operations (compute, merge, computeIfAbsent), how it reaches high concurrency, copy-on-write lists for read-mostly listener lists, concurrent queues and skip lists, and why synchronized wrappers are rarely the answer.

async-virtual-threads.blurb: Three ways to handle many waiting tasks: blocking threads, asynchronous code with futures and callbacks (CompletableFuture composition, timeouts, error handling), event loops, and Java 21 virtual threads that make blocking code cheap again; when each fits and the traps of each.

timers-scheduling.blurb: How programs run work later or periodically: ScheduledExecutorService (fixed rate versus fixed delay), DelayQueue and priority queues of deadlines, hashed timing wheels for millions of timers (timeouts, retries, expiries), and the design of an in-process task scheduler with cancellation and clock handling.

concurrency-puzzles.blurb: The classic concurrency coding questions and the shape of each solution: print in order, alternate threads (FizzBuzz, foo/bar, odd/even, zero-even-odd), H2O, dining philosophers, readers–writers, the sleeping barber, a thread-safe bounded counter and a multithreaded web crawler, with which primitive fits each.

linear-algebra-ml.blurb: Vectors, dot products, matrices as transformations, matrix multiplication shapes, eigenvectors and the SVD: the language every model is written in, with the geometric picture behind each idea.

calculus-gradients.blurb: Derivatives as slopes, partial derivatives and the gradient, the chain rule that powers backpropagation, Jacobians for vector functions, and the second-derivative picture of curvature that explains learning rates.

probability-ml.blurb: Random variables, the distributions ML uses, Bayes' rule, maximum likelihood and MAP estimation (and why they give you MSE, log-loss and regularisation), and entropy, cross-entropy and KL divergence.

statistics-tests.blurb: Sampling, the central limit theorem, standard errors and confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and p-values, power and sample size, and the multiple-testing traps that come up whenever you compare models or run experiments.

ml-framing.blurb: Turning a product goal into a machine-learning task: when ML is the right tool, supervised versus unsupervised versus reinforcement learning, choosing the prediction target, the label and the objective, and the heuristics-first baseline.

bias-variance.blurb: What generalisation means, underfitting versus overfitting, the bias–variance decomposition derived, learning curves for diagnosis, and why huge neural networks break the old U-shaped picture (double descent).

validation-leakage.blurb: Train, validation and test splits and what each is for, k-fold and time-based cross-validation, grouping, the many forms of data leakage, and how to keep evaluation honest when you tune.

loss-functions.blurb: The losses you will be asked about, derived from what each assumes about the data: squared, absolute, Huber and quantile for regression; log-loss, softmax cross-entropy, hinge and focal for classification; ranking and contrastive losses; with their gradients and when each one breaks.

regularisation.blurb: Everything that stops a model from memorising: L2 (weight decay) and L1 penalties and why L1 gives zeros, elastic net, early stopping, data augmentation, dropout, ensembling, and how to tune regularisation strength.

data-labels.blurb: Where training data comes from in real products, logging for ML, label quality and rater agreement, sampling strategies and their biases, selection and feedback effects, and how much data you need.

class-imbalance.blurb: Why rare positives break naive training and evaluation, the metrics to use instead, resampling (undersampling, oversampling, SMOTE), class weights and focal loss, threshold tuning, and recalibrating afterwards.

feature-engineering.blurb: Turning raw data into model inputs: scaling numbers, encoding categories (one-hot, hashing, embeddings, target encoding), crosses, text and time features, aggregates over windows, missing values, and the training–serving skew that ruins production models.

linear-regression.blurb: Fitting a straight line (or plane) by least squares: the normal equations derived, gradient descent as the alternative, what the coefficients mean, the assumptions and how they fail, R² and residual plots, and when linear models are still the right tool.

logistic-regression.blurb: Predicting probabilities with the sigmoid, log-odds and what weights mean, the log-loss gradient derived, the linear decision boundary, softmax regression for many classes, regularisation and calibration, and a from-scratch implementation.

decision-trees.blurb: How a decision tree chooses splits (Gini impurity, entropy and information gain, variance reduction), why single trees overfit, pruning, and how bagging and random forests turn many unstable trees into one strong, robust model.

gradient-boosting.blurb: Boosting as gradient descent in function space: fitting each new tree to the residuals (negative gradients), shrinkage, the XGBoost objective with second-order terms and regularised leaves, LightGBM and CatBoost tricks, tuning, and why it dominates tabular ML.

svm-knn-bayes.blurb: Three classic models interviewers still ask about: support vector machines (maximum margin, hinge loss, the kernel trick), k-nearest neighbours (distance, k, the curse of dimensionality) and naive Bayes (Bayes' rule with an independence assumption), with when each is the right choice.

clustering-pca.blurb: Unsupervised learning you will be asked about: k-means (Lloyd's algorithm, k-means++, choosing k), Gaussian mixtures and EM, hierarchical and density-based clustering, PCA derived as variance maximisation, and t-SNE and UMAP for visualisation.

classification-metrics.blurb: The confusion matrix and everything built from it: precision, recall, F1, specificity, ROC and PR curves and their areas, choosing thresholds, multi-class averaging, log-loss, and calibration with reliability diagrams.

ranking-metrics.blurb: Measuring ranked lists for search, feeds and recommendations: precision and recall at k, hit rate, MRR, MAP, and NDCG with graded relevance derived step by step, plus offline-vs-online gaps, coverage, diversity and novelty.

regression-business-metrics.blurb: Regression metrics (MAE, RMSE, MAPE and its traps, R², quantile coverage), choosing one from the cost of errors, and connecting model metrics to product, guardrail and long-term business metrics.

ab-testing-ml.blurb: Running online experiments for ML models: randomisation units, metrics and guardrails, sample sizing, novelty and network effects, interleaving, shadow mode and canaries, bandits, and why offline wins often vanish online.

mlp-activations.blurb: From one neuron to multi-layer networks: weighted sums, why non-linear activations are essential, sigmoid, tanh, ReLU, leaky ReLU, GELU and SiLU compared, the softmax output layer, universal approximation, and why depth beats width.

backpropagation.blurb: Backpropagation derived for a two-layer network and then in general: the computational graph, forward and backward passes, local gradients and upstream gradients, the matrix-calculus shapes, why it costs only about twice a forward pass, and the vanishing and exploding gradient problems.

optimisers.blurb: Gradient descent variants that train real networks: stochastic and mini-batch SGD, momentum and Nesterov, AdaGrad, RMSProp, Adam and AdamW with their update rules and bias correction, learning-rate warmup and schedules, batch size effects, and how to choose.

init-normalisation.blurb: Keeping signals healthy through deep networks: Xavier and He initialisation derived from variance, batch normalisation (train vs inference behaviour), layer norm and RMSNorm, pre-norm vs post-norm transformers, and residual connections.

training-debugging.blurb: A practical playbook for getting a neural network to train: start small and overfit one batch, read loss curves, diagnose the common failures (NaNs, plateaus, overfitting, data bugs), regularise deep networks, tune hyperparameters, and make runs reproducible.

tensors-autograd.blurb: PyTorch tensors from the ground up: shapes, dtypes and devices, views versus copies, broadcasting rules, indexing and einsum, and how autograd records operations and computes gradients, including the leaf, detach and no_grad details interviews probe.

training-loop.blurb: Writing a correct PyTorch training loop: Dataset and DataLoader, nn.Module, the five-line step, train and eval modes, validation, checkpointing, gradient accumulation and clipping, schedulers, and the structure interviewers expect in an ML coding round.

pytorch-performance.blurb: Making training and inference fast and fit in memory: how GPUs work at a high level, compute-bound versus memory-bound operations and arithmetic intensity, mixed precision (fp16, bf16, loss scaling), torch.compile and kernel fusion, profiling, and memory-saving tricks.

convolution-basics.blurb: What a convolution computes, why weight sharing and locality suit images, output-size arithmetic with padding and stride, channels and parameter counts, pooling, receptive fields, and 1×1 and depthwise-separable convolutions.

cnn-architectures.blurb: The architectures that shaped vision and the idea each introduced: LeNet, AlexNet, VGG, Inception, ResNet and its bottleneck blocks, DenseNet, MobileNet and EfficientNet scaling, ConvNeXt, and Vision Transformers, plus transfer learning in practice.

detection-segmentation.blurb: Beyond classification: object detection (bounding boxes, IoU, anchors, two-stage Faster R-CNN versus one-stage YOLO/SSD, non-maximum suppression, mAP), DETR-style set prediction, and semantic, instance and panoptic segmentation with U-Net and Mask R-CNN.

word2vec.blurb: Why one-hot vectors fail, the distributional hypothesis, word2vec's skip-gram and CBOW objectives with negative sampling derived, what embedding arithmetic shows, GloVe and fastText, and how the same idea gives item and user embeddings.

contrastive-embeddings.blurb: How modern embedding models are trained: contrastive learning and the InfoNCE loss derived, in-batch and hard negatives, temperature, bi-encoders versus cross-encoders, sentence-embedding models and benchmarks, and fine-tuning embeddings for your domain.

embedding-similarity.blurb: Using embeddings well: cosine, dot product and Euclidean distance and when they agree, normalisation and anisotropy, choosing dimensions and compressing (PCA, quantisation, Matryoshka), versioning and drift, and evaluating embeddings.

collaborative-filtering.blurb: Recommending from behaviour alone: user–item matrices, neighbourhood methods, matrix factorisation derived (ALS and SGD), implicit feedback with confidence weights, and the content-based and hybrid alternatives.

two-tower-retrieval.blurb: The multi-stage recommendation funnel and its first stage: two-tower models with user and item towers, in-batch softmax with sampling-bias correction, training data and negatives, serving with ANN indexes, and multiple candidate sources.

ranking-models.blurb: The ranking stage: pointwise, pairwise and listwise learning to rank, CTR prediction models from logistic regression to Wide & Deep, DCN and DLRM, sequence features, multi-task heads (MMoE) and combining their predictions into one score, plus calibration and serving.

recsys-problems.blurb: The problems that make recommenders hard in production: cold start for users and items, exploration with bandits, position and popularity bias, feedback loops and filter bubbles, diversity and re-ranking, freshness, and long-term objectives.

bpe-wordpiece.blurb: Why language models read subword tokens, the byte-pair encoding algorithm step by step (training and encoding), byte-level BPE, WordPiece and the Unigram/SentencePiece approach, special tokens, and implementing a BPE trainer.

tokenization-effects.blurb: How tokenization shapes cost, context length and behaviour: tokens per word across languages, numbers and arithmetic, code and whitespace, spelling and character-level tasks, glitch tokens, and practical token-budget estimates for system design.

self-attention.blurb: Scaled dot-product attention built up from intuition to formula: queries, keys and values, why we scale by the square root of the key dimension, softmax weights, causal masking, the shapes and the quadratic cost, and a from-scratch implementation.

transformer-block.blurb: From one attention head to a full transformer layer: multi-head attention and why heads specialise, the feed-forward block, residual stream and normalisation, the full decoder stack with embeddings and output head, parameter and FLOP counting, and a GPT block in PyTorch.

positional-encodings.blurb: How transformers know word order: absolute sinusoidal and learned position embeddings, relative positions, rotary position embedding (RoPE) derived as rotations, ALiBi linear biases, and extending context length with RoPE scaling.

transformer-families.blurb: The three transformer families and their training objectives: encoder-only (BERT, masked language modelling), decoder-only (GPT, next-token prediction) and encoder–decoder (T5, span corruption), with what each is good at and why decoder-only won for LLMs.

efficient-attention.blurb: Making attention fast and long: FlashAttention's tiling and online softmax, multi-query and grouped-query attention to shrink the KV cache, sliding-window and sparse attention, linear-attention and state-space alternatives, and how long-context models are actually built.

mixture-of-experts.blurb: Sparse mixture-of-experts transformers: replacing the feed-forward block with many experts and a router, top-k gating, load-balancing losses and capacity, expert parallelism, active versus total parameters, and the serving trade-offs.

pretraining-data.blurb: Where LLM pretraining data comes from and how it is cleaned: web crawls, code, books and papers, extraction, language identification, quality filtering, deduplication, toxicity and PII removal, data mixtures and curriculum, contamination, and synthetic data.

scaling-laws.blurb: How loss falls with parameters, data and compute: the Kaplan power laws, compute C ≈ 6ND, Chinchilla's compute-optimal ratio of about 20 tokens per parameter, why modern models over-train for cheaper inference, emergent abilities debated, and using small runs to predict big ones.

distributed-training.blurb: Training models that don't fit on one GPU: data parallelism and all-reduce, ZeRO stages and FSDP, tensor (intra-layer) parallelism, pipeline parallelism and its bubble, sequence and context parallelism, 3-D/4-D parallelism layouts, communication costs, and fault tolerance at thousands of GPUs.

training-memory.blurb: Where training memory goes and how to shrink it: weights, gradients, optimiser state (16 bytes per parameter with Adam in mixed precision), activations and their dependence on batch and sequence length, activation checkpointing, and memory-saving optimisers and precisions.

sft-chat.blurb: Turning a base model into an assistant with supervised fine-tuning: instruction data and where it comes from, chat templates and special tokens, loss masking on prompts, data quality over quantity, multi-turn and tool-use data, and what SFT can and can't fix.

rlhf-ppo.blurb: Reinforcement learning from human feedback: collecting preference comparisons, training a reward model with the Bradley–Terry loss, optimising the policy with PPO against a KL penalty to the reference model, reward hacking, and RLAIF and constitutional AI.

dpo-preferences.blurb: Direct preference optimisation derived from the RLHF objective: the closed-form optimal policy, the implicit reward, the DPO loss and its gradient, β, and the family of offline and online preference methods (IPO, KTO, ORPO, SimPO, online DPO), with their failure modes.

chain-of-thought.blurb: Getting models to reason by spending more computation at answer time: chain-of-thought prompting and why it helps, self-consistency voting, best-of-N with verifiers, tree search, and the test-time compute trade-off between thinking longer and using a bigger model.

reasoning-rl.blurb: How reasoning models are trained: reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards on maths and code, policy-gradient basics, GRPO's group-relative advantages, outcome versus process reward models, rejection-sampling fine-tuning, distillation of reasoning, and the failure modes of RL on language models.
